question: A city government proposes an AI system that would assign residents a general trustworthiness rating from unrelated public records, used by multiple departments to decide access to discretionary services. Under a risk-tiered AI regulatory framework, what is the most likely classification?
options: A. Minimal risk, because every one of the underlying records is already available to the public on request.
B. Limited risk, requiring only that residents are told a rating exists.
C. High risk, permitted once a conformity assessment has been completed.
D. A prohibited practice, because general social scoring by public authorities is banned.
rationale: Risk-tiered frameworks reserve an outright prohibition for a small set of practices, and general social scoring of individuals by public authorities across unrelated contexts is among them. Prohibited means unavailable at any level of documentation, which is why the high-risk answer is wrong: a conformity assessment cannot license a practice the framework forbids.

question: A European distributor buys an AI-enabled inspection system built by a manufacturer outside the region and resells it unchanged under the original brand. The distributor believes obligations rest entirely with the manufacturer. Is that correct?
options: A. No — importers and distributors carry duties of their own.
B. Yes — obligations attach only to the provider that developed and trained the system.
C. Yes — reselling without modification transfers all responsibility to the end deployer.
D. No — reselling a system unchanged makes the distributor the provider for all regulatory purposes.
rationale: AI-specific law differentiates obligations by organisational context: providers, deployers, importers and distributors each carry duties. An importer or distributor must satisfy itself that required documentation and conformity steps exist before placing a system on the market. It does not thereby become the provider, which is why the fourth option overstates the position as badly as the first two understate it.

question: A company is preparing a high-risk AI system for the EU market. Select the three obligations that must be satisfied before the system is placed on the market.
options: A. A conformity assessment appropriate to the system's classification.
B. Publication of the model's full training dataset for independent inspection.
C. Technical documentation sufficient to demonstrate the system meets its requirements.
D. A risk management process operating across the system's lifecycle.
E. Certification of the developing organisation against an information security standard.
rationale: Conformity assessment, technical documentation and lifecycle risk management are core pre-market requirements for high-risk systems, alongside data governance and record keeping. Publishing the training dataset is not required and would often be unlawful, and no AI framework conditions market access on the developer holding an information security certification.

question: A team is designing a model that flags university applications for manual review. Engineering proposes optimising for overall accuracy and setting the review threshold once the model is trained. What should governance require instead?
options: A. That overall accuracy be replaced entirely by a single fairness metric as the model's optimisation target.
B. That the threshold be set by whichever value produces the fewest manual reviews.
C. That success metrics and thresholds be defined during design, across applicant groups.
D. That the model be trained on the full applicant history before any metric is chosen.
rationale: Metric and threshold evaluation is a design-phase activity, not a post-training adjustment. Choosing them beforehand fixes what the system is trying to achieve and how failure will be recognised, including how error is distributed across groups. Replacing accuracy outright, minimising workload, or deferring until after training all let the metric be chosen to flatter the result.

question: A government agency is designing an AI system to prioritise applications for a hardship benefit. The design team is drawn entirely from engineering and finance. Which design-phase activity is most clearly missing?
options: A. A benchmark comparing the planned model against the commercially available alternatives on the market.
B. Stakeholder engagement with caseworkers and applicant representatives.
C. A pilot restricted to applications already approved through the manual process.
D. A decision on whether the model will run on agency infrastructure or in the cloud.
rationale: Stakeholder engagement and feedback is a named part of applying policies and best practice when designing a system. The people who administer the benefit and those who receive it hold information about failure modes that engineering and finance cannot supply. Benchmarking, pilot scope and hosting are real decisions that do not surface who the design might harm.

question: A payments company has finished testing a fraud model and the team wants to release. Governance asks what has to be true before production. Which answer best describes a release readiness gate?
options: A. That the model outperformed the incumbent on the held-out test set.
B. That the engineering team has the capacity to support the system through the months after launch.
C. That the release date has been communicated to affected internal teams.
D. That defined criteria — performance, documentation, conformity, rollback — are met and recorded.
rationale: Assessing readiness and preparing for release means testing the release against criteria agreed in advance and recording the result, so that a go decision is auditable and a no-go is possible. Beating the incumbent is one input among several, and support capacity and internal communication are launch logistics rather than a readiness standard.

question: A retailer's recommendation model is retrained nightly from live customer interactions. Security asks what periodic assessment should cover beyond ordinary performance monitoring.
options: A. Threat modelling and adversarial testing of the training pipeline.
B. Renegotiation of the cloud hosting agreement in order to secure improved availability terms overall.
C. Verification that recommendation latency remains within the agreed service target.
D. Confirmation that the model's accuracy has not fallen below its launch measurement.
rationale: Periodic activities to assess a system include audits, red teaming, threat modelling and security testing. A pipeline that learns continuously from user-influenced data is exposed to deliberate manipulation of its training inputs, which no accuracy or latency measure detects. Hosting terms are commercial, and latency and accuracy are the ordinary monitoring the question already excludes.

question: A logistics company's route optimisation model begins producing unusable routes for one region. Engineering identifies the immediate cause within a day. What does governance require beyond the fix?
options: A. Suspension of the model in all regions until the fix has run for a full quarter.
B. Reassignment of model ownership to the regional operations team most affected by the failure itself.
C. Documentation of the incident and cross-functional review of why it arose.
D. A public statement describing the failure and the corrective action taken.
rationale: Managing and documenting incidents, and collaborating with cross-functional stakeholders to understand why they arise — brittleness, data quality, insufficient testing, drift — is a named maintenance responsibility. The immediate cause explains the symptom; the review explains why controls did not catch it. Global suspension, reassignment and public disclosure are responses to different problems.

question: An energy utility retrains its demand model only when someone notices the forecasts have become unreliable. Over two years this has happened three times, each after weeks of degraded output. What should replace this practice?
options: A. A policy of retraining the model immediately after any forecast miss exceeds tolerance once.
B. Continuous monitoring with a defined maintenance, update and retraining schedule.
C. A switch to a simpler statistical model that is less sensitive to changing conditions.
D. An annual external audit of the model's forecasting performance and methodology.
rationale: Conducting continuous monitoring and establishing a regular schedule for maintenance, updates and retraining is the named control. Waiting for someone to notice guarantees weeks of degraded output every time. Retraining on a single miss overreacts to noise, replacing the model abandons capability to avoid a maintenance problem, and an annual audit would detect the drift long after it caused harm.

question: A law firm wants an AI assistant that summarises privileged client documents. Confidentiality obligations prevent client material leaving firm-controlled infrastructure. Which deployment consideration follows most directly?
options: A. The assistant should be limited to documents drawn from client matters that have already concluded.
B. The firm should require every lawyer to review each summary before it is relied upon.
C. The firm should select the largest available model to minimise summarisation errors.
D. Deployment options must be evaluated, favouring on-premise or private hosting.
rationale: Understanding the differences in deployment options — cloud, on-premise, edge — is part of evaluating a deployment decision, and a constraint that data must not leave controlled infrastructure resolves directly to where the model runs. Restricting to closed matters, mandating review and choosing a larger model are all reasonable practices that leave the confidentiality constraint unaddressed.

question: An insurer needs to predict claim severity from twelve structured fields with a decade of labelled history. A team proposes a large language model. What is the strongest governance objection?
options: A. A model type poorly matched to a structured task adds opacity and cost.
B. Language models cannot be applied to numerical data under any circumstances.
C. Insurance regulators prohibit generative models in all claims-related processes.
D. The decade of historical claims data would first have to be converted into natural language form.
rationale: Understanding the differences between model types — classic versus generative among them — is part of the deployment decision. A well-understood tabular problem with abundant labels is where classic approaches are strongest and most explainable; reaching for a generative model imports opacity, cost and evaluation difficulty for no gain. The alternatives state prohibitions and technical impossibilities that do not exist.

question: A company wants an internal assistant to answer questions from an engineering handbook that is revised most weeks. Accuracy against the current text matters more than writing style. Which approach best fits?
options: A. Fine-tune a base model on the handbook and repeat the fine-tune after each revision.
B. Deploy the base model unchanged and instruct staff to verify answers against the handbook.
C. Use retrieval against the current handbook at query time, leaving the base model unmodified.
D. Train a model from scratch on the handbook so that no external content can influence answers.
rationale: Deployment options include using a model as is, fine-tuning it, or applying retrieval, and the choice follows the requirement. Content that changes weekly and must be answered accurately points to retrieval, which reads the current text at query time. Repeated fine-tuning is expensive and always lags, unmodified deployment does not know the handbook, and training from scratch is disproportionate.

question: A distribution business is deciding whether to deploy a third-party AI system for warehouse staffing. Select the three factors most relevant to the deployment decision itself.
options: A. Whether the intended use case is clearly defined with measurable business objectives.
B. Whether the vendor's user interface matches the company's internal design conventions.
C. Whether data of sufficient quality and availability exists to support the intended use.
D. Whether the workforce is prepared to operate and question the system appropriately.
E. Whether the vendor's engineering team is larger than that of competing suppliers.
rationale: Understanding the context of the use case covers business objectives, performance requirements, data availability, ethical considerations and workforce readiness. Interface conventions are an aesthetic preference, and supplier headcount is not evidence about the system being bought.

question: A vendor supplies its own completed impact assessment for an AI scheduling system and asks the buyer to accept it as satisfying the buyer's assessment obligation. How should the buyer respond?
options: A. Accept it, since the vendor understands the system's internals better than the buyer can.
B. Review it and perform its own assessment of the system as deployed in its context.
C. Reject it and commission an independent third party to repeat the work from scratch.
D. Accept it on condition the vendor indemnifies the buyer against any assessment error.
rationale: Performing or reviewing an impact assessment on the selected system is the deployer's activity. A vendor assessment is useful evidence about the system in general, but it cannot cover the buyer's population, use case or controls, which is where the impact actually lands. Wholesale acceptance skips the part only the buyer can do; commissioning a third party to start over discards useful work; and an indemnity transfers cost, not the obligation.
